title: Advanced React Architecture
description: Go beyond Module 6's React fundamentals into the architectural patterns real production codebases rely on: composition-based component design, custom hooks for reusable logic, advanced Context patterns, performance optimization, code splitting, and the production checklist that separates a working React app from a genuinely scalable one.

moduleGoal.primary: Master composition-based component architecture and custom hooks as the primary tools for organizing and reusing logic in a growing React codebase.
moduleGoal.secondary: Diagnose and fix real React performance problems using memoization and code splitting, and develop the architectural judgment that distinguishes a React app that merely works from one genuinely ready for production scale.
moduleGoal.outcomeStatement: By the end of this module, you will be able to architect a React codebase the way experienced React engineers do: composing rather than configuring, extracting reusable logic into custom hooks, and diagnosing performance problems with precision rather than guesswork.

lessons.title: Component Architecture Patterns
lessons.lessonGoal: Move beyond Module 6's basic component boundaries into deliberate composition patterns: the children prop, compound components, and the render-prop-like 'children as a function' pattern.

sections.title: Composition As React's Primary Extension Mechanism
sections.content: Module 6, lesson 3 briefly mentioned the children prop as a way for a component to render whatever JSX is passed between its opening and closing tags. This lesson treats composition — building complex UI by combining smaller, flexible components together, rather than building large, configurable components with many specific props — as React's primary, idiomatic mechanism for reuse and flexibility, directly extending Module 6, lesson 10's component-boundary thinking into the deliberate, architectural patterns experienced React engineers reach for by default. Where a beginner instinct (and Module 6's own simpler examples) might add more and more specific props to a component to handle more cases, composition instead asks: could this component simply accept arbitrary children, or a small number of specifically-shaped child components, and let the caller compose the actual structure themselves?

sections.title: A Picture Frame Versus A Custom-Built Display Case For Every Possible Item
sections.content: A component with many specific configuration props, trying to handle every possible use case through props alone, is like commissioning an entirely custom-built display case for every single item you might ever want to display — technically possible, but each new item type requires a new custom case, and the case-maker (the component's author) must anticipate every future need in advance. A composable component is like a simple, well-made picture frame: it doesn't know or care what's inside it, it simply provides consistent framing, spacing, and presentation, and accepts literally anything placed inside — a photo, a certificate, a child's drawing — without ever needing to be redesigned for each new kind of content. Most real UI components benefit far more from being a flexible 'frame' (accepting children) than from being an ever-more-elaborate 'custom display case' (accepting dozens of specific configuration props for every conceivable variation).

sections.title: Core Composition Patterns
Why Compound Components Need Context, And How The Pieces Actually Connect
sections.content: A compound component like Tabs works specifically because its sub-components (Tabs.Tab, Tabs.Panel) need to share state — which tab is currently active — without that state being threaded down as an explicit prop on every single sub-component usage, exactly the prop-drilling problem Module 10, lesson 3 introduced Context to solve generally. The parent Tabs component creates a Context provider internally, holding the active tab state; each Tabs.Tab and Tabs.Panel calls useContext internally to read and (for Tabs.Tab specifically) update that shared state, without the actual JSX usage ever needing to manually pass activeTab or setActiveTab as visible props anywhere. This is precisely why Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab, and Tabs.Panel are typically defined as properties attached to the Tabs function itself (Tabs.Tab = TabComponent) — a deliberate convention signaling 'these components are designed to be used together, inside a parent Tabs, and rely on that specific context being present'.

sections.title: A Complete Compound Tabs Component, Built From Scratch
sections.content: This builds a genuinely working compound component, directly extending Module 6's Context patterns and Module 10, lesson 3's AuthContext structure into a reusable UI pattern:
sections.explanation: useTabsContext deliberately throws an error if called outside a Tabs provider, directly extending Module 7, lesson 9's error-handling discipline into a component-design safeguard — a clear, immediate error ('must be used inside Tabs') is far more useful to a future developer than a confusing null-reference failure somewhere deep inside Tab or Panel. Panel's conditional rendering (if (activeTab !== id) return null;) directly reuses Module 6, lesson 7's early-return conditional pattern, just applied here based on shared Context state rather than a prop. The Tabs.List = TabsList; assignments at the bottom are what let callers write <Tabs.Tab> instead of needing to separately import and use a differently-named TabComponent, completing the compound component's intended, cohesive API.

sections.title: Where Composition Patterns Dominate Real Component Libraries
sections.content: Nearly every major, widely-used React component library relies heavily on exactly these composition patterns — compound components for things like tabs, accordions, dropdown menus, and modals, specifically because these UI patterns inherently involve multiple coordinated pieces that benefit from sharing implicit state without forcing every consumer to manually wire that coordination themselves. Real component library authors specifically favor composition over an ever-growing list of configuration props because composition scales better as new use cases emerge: a new way of arranging Tabs.Tab and Tabs.Panel rarely requires changing Tabs's own implementation at all, where a props-heavy approach would likely require adding yet another specific configuration prop for every new arrangement anyone wants to support.

sections.title: Common Composition Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Continuing to add more and more specific configuration props to a component to handle every new variation, rather than recognizing when composition (accepting children, or specific compound sub-components) would scale far better as genuine variety grows.

2. Building a compound component's sub-components as entirely separate, independently-exported functions rather than attaching them to the parent (Tabs.Tab = Tab), losing the clear, cohesive API signal that these pieces are specifically meant to be used together.

3. Forgetting to guard against a sub-component being used outside its required parent context, leading to a confusing null-reference error rather than this lesson's clear, immediate 'must be used inside X' error.

4. Over-applying compound component patterns to genuinely simple components that don't actually need shared implicit state, adding unnecessary architectural complexity where a simple, ordinary component with regular props would have been clearer and easier to use.

5. Forgetting that children is itself just a regular prop (typed as React.ReactNode in TypeScript, Module 12's typing applied here directly) — it isn't special syntax, just a conventionally-named, automatically-populated prop representing whatever JSX appears between a component's opening and closing tags.

sections.title: Composition Over Configuration, Applied To Component Design Specifically
sections.content: This lesson's central argument is a direct, component-design-specific application of the exact same 'convention over configuration' principle Module 13, lesson 2 introduced for Next.js's file-based routing: rather than requiring every possible variation to be explicitly configured through props (configuration), composition lets the CALLER assemble exactly the structure they need from smaller, flexible pieces, with the underlying component simply providing consistent behavior and shared state where genuinely needed. This same instinct — recognizing when a growing list of specific configuration options signals a deeper need for a more flexible, composable structure instead — is one of the most valuable, transferable architectural judgments a React engineer develops with experience, and it applies well beyond components specifically, to API design, function design, and system design generally.

sections.title: Diagnosing Compound Component Context Errors
sections.content: If a compound component's sub-component throws the 'must be used inside X' error this lesson's codeLesson deliberately added, the fix is almost always confirming that sub-component is genuinely rendered as a descendant of its required parent provider somewhere in the actual JSX tree — exactly the same diagnostic Module 10, lesson 3 taught for any Context consumer rendered outside its Provider's boundaries. If a compound component's shared state doesn't seem to update correctly across its sub-components, confirming the Context value object passed to the Provider is actually being recreated correctly on each render (rather than accidentally creating a new, disconnected context value somewhere) is the next thing to check.

checkpoints.question: What is the main architectural advantage of composition (accepting children or compound sub-components) over an ever-growing list of specific configuration props?
options: Composition always results in less code overall regardless of the situation
Composition lets the caller assemble exactly the structure they need from flexible pieces, scaling better as new use cases emerge than continually adding new configuration props
Configuration props are never a valid approach in React
Composition eliminates the need for any props at all
checkpoints.explanation: Composition lets callers flexibly assemble structure from smaller pieces, which tends to scale better as new variations emerge than an ever-growing list of specific configuration props on one component.

checkpoints.question: A compound component's Tab sub-component is accidentally rendered outside of its required parent Tabs provider, and the component throws a clear error stating 'Tab must be used inside Tabs'. Why is this preferable to a confusing null-reference error?
options: There is no real difference between the two kinds of errors

A clear, immediate, descriptive error directly tells a future developer exactly what went wrong and how to fix it, rather than requiring them to trace a confusing failure back to its actual root cause themselves
Null-reference errors are always more helpful than custom errors
This kind of error checking is unnecessary in well-written code
checkpoints.explanation: A deliberate, descriptive error message immediately communicates the actual problem and its fix, saving a future developer from needing to trace a more generic, confusing failure back to its root cause.

checkpoints.question: Why are a compound component's sub-components (like Tabs.Tab) typically attached directly to the parent component function rather than exported as entirely separate, independently-named functions?
options: React requires this exact syntax for all components
It creates a clear, cohesive API signal that these specific pieces are designed to be used together, inside the parent component, rather than appearing as unrelated, independent exports
This has no real benefit and is purely a stylistic preference
Separate exports are always faster at runtime
checkpoints.explanation: Attaching sub-components to the parent (Tabs.Tab) signals their intended relationship clearly, communicating that they're meant to be used together as part of one cohesive compound component.

codingChallenge.title: Build A Compound Accordion Component
codingChallenge.description: Build a compound Accordion component (Accordion, Accordion.Item, Accordion.Header, Accordion.Content) where exactly one item can be expanded at a time, using Context internally to share the currently-expanded item's id, with a clear error if a sub-component is used outside Accordion.
validationRules: Must use Context internally to share expandedId across sub-components
useAccordionContext must throw a clear, descriptive error if called outside the provider
Header must toggle expandedId, collapsing if the same id is clicked again
Content must conditionally render only when its id matches expandedId
Header and Content must be attached to Accordion (Accordion.Header, Accordion.Content)
hints: Only one item should ever be expanded at once, since expandedId is a single value, not an array or set
Clicking the currently expanded item's header again should collapse it (set expandedId back to null)
Reuse this lesson's exact Tabs pattern structurally, just renamed for an accordion's specific behavior

lessons.title: Custom Hooks
lessons.lessonGoal: Extract reusable stateful logic into custom hooks, understanding the Rules of Hooks deeply enough to build your own, and recognizing exactly when logic genuinely warrants extraction.

sections.title: Custom Hooks As Reusable Stateful Logic, Not Reusable UI
sections.content: Module 6, lesson 5 used useState and useEffect together repeatedly for data fetching, and Module 10, lesson 2 noted that custom hooks (briefly mentioned there) bundle related state and effect logic together. This lesson builds that concept fully: a custom hook is simply a regular JavaScript function, conventionally named starting with 'use', that itself calls other hooks (useState, useEffect, or other custom hooks) internally — letting you extract and reuse STATEFUL LOGIC across multiple components, distinct from lesson 1's composition patterns, which reuse UI STRUCTURE. Where a compound component shares rendered JSX and structure, a custom hook shares the underlying logic (loading states, event listeners, calculations) while leaving each component free to render that logic's results however it specifically needs to.

sections.title: A Reusable Recipe, Not A Reusable Finished Dish
sections.content: Lesson 1's composition patterns are like a reusable, pre-plated dish (a Card component) — you get both the food and its specific presentation together, as one unit. A custom hook is more like a reusable RECIPE: the actual cooking process (the logic — how to fetch data, how to track a timer, how to detect a click outside an element) is written once and reused, but each 'chef' (each component using the hook) is free to plate and present the resulting dish however they specifically need to for their own particular situation. Two completely different-looking components could both use the exact same useFetch custom hook internally, sharing 100% of the actual data-fetching logic while rendering the loading, error, and success states in entirely different, component-specific ways.

sections.title: Building And Using A Custom Hook
The Rules Of Hooks, And Why Custom Hooks Must Follow Them Too
sections.content: Module 6, lesson 5 briefly mentioned the Rules of Hooks (always call hooks at the top level, never conditionally or inside loops). Custom hooks don't get any exemption from these rules — since a custom hook is, underneath its own name, just calling React's actual built-in hooks internally, every one of those internal calls (useState, useEffect) must still follow the exact same rules as if they were called directly inside a component. This is precisely why useFetch's internal useState and useEffect calls appear unconditionally, at the top level of the function, exactly as they would inside a regular component — a custom hook is, in this very specific sense, indistinguishable from a component's own body as far as React's hook-calling rules are concerned, it simply isn't returning JSX. This also explains why a custom hook must itself be called only from another hook or from a component's own top level, never from inside a regular helper function or conditionally — the same rule, just one level removed.

sections.title: A Second, Genuinely Different Custom Hook: useLocalStorage
sections.content: This builds a different custom hook entirely, directly extending Module 5's To-Do App project's localStorage pattern into a genuinely reusable, generic hook:
sections.explanation: useLocalStorage's initial useState call uses a lazy initializer function (() => { ... }) specifically so the relatively expensive localStorage read only happens once, on the component's first render, rather than on every single re-render — a small but genuine performance detail lesson 4 will revisit in more depth. Returning [value, setValue] as const (TypeScript's const assertion, ensuring the returned tuple's exact order and types are preserved correctly) lets this hook be used with the EXACT same destructuring syntax as React's own useState, making it feel like a natural, drop-in extension of a pattern developers already know intuitively. Notice TodoApp's addTask function contains zero manual localStorage code at all — every bit of that logic, including the actual persistence, lives once, inside the hook, completely hidden from and unnecessary for any component using it to think about.

sections.title: Common, Real Custom Hooks Across Production Codebases
sections.content: Real production React codebases accumulate a library of custom hooks addressing extremely common, recurring needs: useFetch or similar data-fetching hooks (often replaced by dedicated data-fetching libraries as a codebase matures, but conceptually identical), useLocalStorage, useDebounce (delaying a value's update until a user has stopped typing for a moment, useful for search inputs), and useMediaQuery (tracking whether the current viewport matches a specific responsive breakpoint, directly connecting to Module 3's responsive design concepts). Many real teams maintain a dedicated hooks/ folder (directly extending Module 10, lesson 9's project structure principles) specifically for these reusable, shared pieces of logic, treating well-designed custom hooks as genuinely valuable, reusable infrastructure rather than one-off conveniences.

sections.title: Common Custom Hook Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Calling a custom hook (or any hook) conditionally, inside an if statement or a loop, violating the Rules of Hooks exactly as this lesson's internalWorking section described, since the custom hook's own internal hook calls inherit this same strict requirement.

2. Extracting logic into a custom hook prematurely, when that logic is only ever actually used in one single component — not every piece of stateful logic needs its own hook; extraction genuinely pays off specifically when logic is reused across multiple components, or when extraction itself meaningfully clarifies one large component's own internal organization.

3. Forgetting the lazy initializer function for an expensive initial useState computation (like useLocalStorage's localStorage.getItem call), causing that expensive computation to run on every single render rather than only once.

4. Naming a function that doesn't actually call any other hooks internally with a 'use' prefix anyway, misleadingly suggesting it's a hook (and subject to the Rules of Hooks) when it's actually just a regular helper function with no such constraints.

5. Building an overly generic, all-purpose custom hook trying to handle too many different specific use cases at once, rather than several smaller, more focused hooks that compose together cleanly — echoing lesson 1's same composition-over-configuration argument, now applied to hooks instead of components.

sections.title: Recognizing Genuine Extraction Opportunities, Not Extracting By Default
sections.content: This lesson's central judgment, directly echoing Module 4, lesson 3's DRY principle but now applied specifically to React's hook model, is recognizing WHEN logic genuinely warrants extraction into its own custom hook, rather than extracting prematurely or reflexively. The signal worth watching for is genuine duplication: if you notice the same useState/useEffect pattern (or a meaningfully similar variant of it) appearing in two or more components, that's the concrete signal lesson 2's extraction pays off, exactly the same 'duplication is the signal, not an aesthetic preference' instinct Module 4 taught for ordinary functions. Extracting a single component's own internal logic into a hook purely for its own sake, with no actual reuse occurring anywhere, often adds an extra layer of indirection without delivering composition's genuine benefit — the same caution this lesson's failureCases section raised explicitly.

sections.title: Diagnosing Custom Hook Bugs
sections.content: If a component using a custom hook misbehaves, the most reliable diagnostic step is testing the custom hook's logic directly, isolated from any specific component's rendering — since a custom hook is just a regular function (that happens to call other hooks), reasoning about its actual logic independent of any particular component's JSX is usually the fastest way to isolate whether a bug lives in the hook's own internal logic or in how a specific component is using that hook's returned values. If you suspect a Rules of Hooks violation (an inconsistent number of hook calls between renders, a common symptom being a confusing 'hooks called in a different order' warning), checking for any conditional or loop-wrapped hook calls — inside the custom hook itself, not just the component using it — is the first thing to check, exactly per this lesson's internalWorking section.

checkpoints.question: What is the key difference between lesson 1's composition patterns and this lesson's custom hooks, in terms of what each one reuses?
options: They are functionally identical, with no real difference
Composition patterns (like compound components) reuse rendered UI structure; custom hooks reuse underlying stateful LOGIC, leaving each component free to render the results however it needs
Custom hooks can only be used for styling, never for logic
Composition patterns can never include any logic at all
checkpoints.explanation: Composition patterns share UI structure and rendering, while custom hooks specifically share reusable stateful logic, independent of how each component using that hook chooses to render its results.

checkpoints.question: A custom hook's internal useState call is placed inside an if statement, only running under certain conditions. What problem does this create?
options: No problem; custom hooks are exempt from the Rules of Hooks
This violates the Rules of Hooks, since a custom hook's internal hook calls must follow the exact same unconditional, top-level-only requirement as hooks called directly inside a component
This only matters if the custom hook is used in more than one component
Conditional hook calls are required for custom hooks specifically
checkpoints.explanation: Custom hooks receive no exemption from the Rules of Hooks; their internal hook calls must remain unconditional and at the top level, exactly like hooks called directly inside any component.

checkpoints.question: According to this lesson, when does extracting logic into a custom hook genuinely pay off?
options: Every single piece of stateful logic should always be extracted into its own custom hook by default
When the same or a meaningfully similar useState/useEffect pattern appears in two or more components, signaling genuine duplication worth extracting
Custom hooks should never actually be used in real projects
Only when a component has no other logic at all
checkpoints.explanation: Genuine duplication across multiple components is the concrete signal that extraction into a custom hook is worthwhile, rather than extracting reflexively or by default for every piece of logic.

codingChallenge.title: Build A useDebounce Custom Hook
codingChallenge.description: Build a generic useDebounce<T> custom hook that returns a debounced version of a value, only updating after a specified delay has passed without the input value changing again, and use it in a search component to avoid firing a search on every single keystroke.
validationRules: useDebounce must be generic (<T>), not restricted to a single specific type
Must use a cleanup function (returned from useEffect) that clears the previous timeout when the value changes again before the delay elapses
SearchBox must use the debounced value (not the raw input value) for the actual search-triggering useEffect
Must correctly include both value and delayMs in the dependency array
hints: The cleanup function returned from useEffect runs before the next effect execution, which is exactly what cancels a pending, now-outdated timeout
Without this cleanup, every keystroke would still eventually trigger a search, just delayed - the cleanup is what actually prevents intermediate values from ever firing
Test mentally: typing 'cat' quickly should only log one search for 'cat', not one for 'c', 'ca', and 'cat' each

lessons.title: Context API Deep Dive
lessons.lessonGoal: Understand Context's real performance characteristics, the multiple-small-contexts pattern, and how to combine Context with a custom hook for a clean, reusable API.

sections.title: Beyond 'How To Use Context' Into 'How Context Actually Behaves'
sections.content: Module 10, lesson 3 taught Context's basic mechanics: createContext, a Provider, and useContext for consuming it, using AuthContext as the running example. This lesson goes deeper into Context's actual runtime behavior — specifically, exactly which components re-render when a context value changes, and the deliberate architectural patterns (splitting one large context into several smaller ones, pairing Context with a custom hook from lesson 2) experienced React engineers use to manage Context at scale, directly building on both lesson 1's composition patterns and lesson 2's custom hooks into one combined, production-grade pattern.

sections.title: A Building-Wide Intercom Versus Several Separate, Targeted Intercoms
sections.content: Module 10, lesson 3 compared Context to a building-wide announcement system. This lesson refines that metaphor with a detail worth understanding precisely: a single, building-wide intercom broadcasting EVERY announcement (user info, theme preference, shopping cart contents, all bundled into one combined context value) means every single room with a receiver hears every single announcement, even ones genuinely irrelevant to that specific room — a room only caring about the building's temperature still has to process every unrelated announcement about packages being delivered. Several separate, targeted intercom channels — one for temperature, one for deliveries, one for emergency alerts — let each room's receiver tune in only to the channels actually relevant to it, processing far less irrelevant noise. This is precisely the architectural argument for splitting Context into several smaller, focused contexts rather than one large, combined one.

sections.title: Splitting Context, And Pairing It With A Custom Hook
Why Every Consumer Of A Context Re-Renders When That Context's Value Changes
sections.content: This is the single most important performance fact about Context to understand precisely: when a Context Provider's value changes, EVERY component calling useContext for that specific context re-renders, regardless of whether that specific component actually uses the particular piece of the value that changed. If AppContextValue bundles user, theme, and cartItems together into one single object, and theme changes, every single component consuming AppContext re-renders — including components that only ever read user and never reference theme at all — simply because the Provider's overall value object is a new object reference each time any piece of it changes. This directly explains this lesson's mental model: splitting into separate AuthContext and ThemeContext means a theme change only re-renders components actually consuming ThemeContext, leaving every AuthContext-only consumer completely unaffected, exactly the targeted-intercom-channel behavior the mental model described.

sections.title: Demonstrating The Re-Render Difference Directly
sections.content: This shows the actual, observable consequence of combined versus split contexts, directly extending Module 6's React Developer Tools debugging habit:
sections.explanation: In the combined-context version, UserGreeting calls useContext(AppContext) directly, meaning it's subscribed to the ENTIRE AppContext value — any change to any piece of that bundled object triggers a re-render here, even though this component only ever reads user. In the split-context version, UserGreeting calls useAuth() (lesson 2's custom hook pattern, wrapping useContext(AuthContext) specifically), meaning it's only ever subscribed to AuthContext — a completely separate ThemeToggle component changing theme via its own, separate ThemeContext has zero effect on UserGreeting's render count at all. This is the concrete, measurable performance payoff this lesson's splitting pattern provides, directly previewing lesson 4's broader performance optimization theme.

sections.title: How Real, Larger React Applications Organize Context
sections.content: Real production React applications with substantial shared state commonly maintain several small, focused contexts (an AuthContext, a ThemeContext, sometimes a NotificationContext or a FeatureFlagContext), each paired with its own custom hook following exactly this lesson's useAuth/useTheme pattern, rather than one combined context attempting to hold everything. Many real teams specifically audit their context usage as an application grows, watching for exactly the kind of unnecessary re-render this lesson's codeLesson demonstrated, using React Developer Tools' Profiler (an extension of the Components panel introduced in Module 6) to directly observe which components re-render in response to which specific state changes, and splitting contexts further whenever an unexpectedly broad set of components turns out to be re-rendering for unrelated reasons.

sections.title: Common Advanced Context Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Bundling many unrelated pieces of state into one single, large context purely for convenience, then being confused by widespread, seemingly unrelated performance problems once the application has many consumers of that one combined context.

2. Calling useContext directly inside many components instead of pairing each context with its own custom hook (this lesson's useAuth/useTheme pattern), losing both the clear, descriptive error-throwing behavior and the consistent, easy-to-refactor API a paired custom hook provides.

3. Assuming splitting contexts is always necessary even for genuinely small, simple applications where this specific performance concern never actually manifests in practice — this is a deliberate optimization for genuine scale, not a rule to apply reflexively to every project regardless of actual size or need.

4. Forgetting that even with split contexts, a context whose value object is recreated unnecessarily on every single render (rather than only when its actual underlying data changes) still causes unnecessary re-renders — splitting context is one optimization, but not the only one relevant to Context performance.

5. Over-engineering an application with many separate contexts from the very start, before any genuine performance problem or even genuine logical separation has emerged, adding architectural complexity disproportionate to the project's actual current needs.

sections.title: Performance-Aware Architecture, Decided Deliberately Rather Than By Default
sections.content: This lesson's central argument directly extends Module 3, lesson 7's animation-performance lesson into React's own component re-render model: two architecturally similar approaches (one combined context, several split contexts) can produce dramatically different real-world performance characteristics, and recognizing which approach fits a SPECIFIC application's actual scale and update patterns is a deliberate architectural judgment, not a reflexive default in either direction. Splitting contexts prematurely, before any genuine need exists, adds real complexity without a corresponding benefit; never splitting them, even as an application's shared state and consumer count genuinely grows, risks exactly the kind of broad, hard-to-diagnose performance problem this lesson's codeLesson demonstrated concretely. This same 'match the architecture's complexity to the application's actual, current scale' judgment recurs throughout this entire module's remaining lessons.

sections.title: Diagnosing Unnecessary Re-Renders Caused By Context
sections.content: React Developer Tools' Profiler tab (an extension of the Components panel) can directly record and display exactly which components re-rendered during a specific interaction, and why — using this to record a single state change (like ThemeToggle's click) and observing whether components that shouldn't logically be affected (like UserGreeting, in this lesson's example) are nonetheless re-rendering is the most direct, evidence-based way to confirm whether an overly broad, combined context is genuinely the cause, rather than guessing based on the code's structure alone. If this kind of unrelated re-rendering is confirmed and is genuinely causing a measurable performance problem (not just a theoretical one), splitting the offending combined context into more focused pieces, exactly per this lesson's structure section, is the direct, standard fix.

checkpoints.question: When a Context Provider's value changes, which components re-render?
options: Only the specific components that use the exact piece of the value that changed
Every component calling useContext for that specific context re-renders, regardless of whether that component actually uses the particular piece of the value that changed
No components re-render automatically; manual re-rendering must be triggered
Only the Provider component itself re-renders
checkpoints.explanation: Every consumer of a given context re-renders whenever that context's value changes, regardless of which specific piece of the bundled value a given component actually uses.

checkpoints.question: An application combines user, theme, and cartItems into one single AppContext. A user toggles the theme, and a component that only ever displays the user's name also re-renders as a result. Why does this happen?
options: This is a React bug that should never occur

Since all three pieces of state are bundled into one single context value, any change to any piece (including theme) causes every consumer of that combined context to re-render, even ones only using an unrelated piece like user
The user's name component has a bug unrelated to context
This only happens if the application has more than 100 components
checkpoints.explanation: Bundling unrelated state into one combined context means any change to any piece causes every consumer to re-render, even those that only use a different, unaffected piece of that bundled value.

checkpoints.question: According to this lesson, when does splitting a large context into several smaller ones genuinely pay off?
options: Always, for every application regardless of size or actual need
When an application has genuine scale and a measurable re-render performance problem traceable to an overly broad, combined context - not as a reflexive default for every small project
Never; splitting context provides no real benefit in any situation
Only when an application has exactly two pieces of shared state
checkpoints.explanation: Splitting context is a deliberate optimization that genuinely pays off at real scale with measurable re-render problems, not a rule to apply reflexively to every project regardless of actual size or need.

codingChallenge.title: Split A Combined Context Into Two Focused Contexts
codingChallenge.description: Given a combined NotificationsAndSettingsContext bundling unread notification count and a user's display-density setting, split it into two separate, focused contexts (NotificationsContext and SettingsContext), each paired with its own custom hook with proper error throwing.
validationRules: Must create two genuinely separate contexts, not one combined context with two consumers
Each context must have its own Provider component managing only its own relevant state
Each context must be paired with its own custom hook (useNotifications, useSettings)
Each custom hook must throw a clear, descriptive error if called outside its corresponding Provider
Changing density must have no effect on anything related to unreadCount, and vice versa
hints: Each Provider should only manage the state genuinely relevant to its own specific context, not anything from the other one
Reuse lesson 1 and lesson 2's exact error-throwing pattern for each custom hook
The key test: could a component using only useNotifications ever re-render due to a density change? It should not be able to.

lessons.title: Performance Optimisation
lessons.lessonGoal: Diagnose React performance problems precisely using the Profiler, and apply React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback correctly and only where genuinely justified by measured evidence.

sections.title: Measuring Before Optimizing
sections.content: Lesson 3 demonstrated one specific cause of unnecessary re-renders (overly broad Context). This lesson covers React's three primary memoization tools — React.memo (skip re-rendering a component if its props haven't changed), useMemo (skip recalculating an expensive value if its dependencies haven't changed), and useCallback (skip recreating a function if its dependencies haven't changed) — but frames every one of them explicitly around this lesson's central, non-negotiable rule: measure first, using React Developer Tools' Profiler, before reaching for any of these tools, since each one carries its own real cost (additional comparison overhead, additional code complexity) that can easily exceed whatever performance problem it was meant to solve, if applied without genuine evidence that a real problem exists.

sections.title: A Doctor Diagnosing Before Prescribing, Not Prescribing By Habit
sections.content: Module 7, lesson 1's opening lesson compared engineering judgment generally to a doctor's diagnostic reasoning. This lesson applies that exact comparison specifically and concretely: a careless doctor might prescribe a specific medication reflexively, by habit, regardless of a patient's actual symptoms; a careful doctor diagnoses first — runs tests, gathers actual evidence — before prescribing anything at all, since the wrong medication, prescribed without genuine justification, can itself cause real harm with no corresponding benefit. React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback are this lesson's 'medications': each one has a genuine, real use case, but reaching for them reflexively, without first 'running the tests' (profiling, measuring actual re-render behavior), risks adding real complexity and overhead to address a problem that may not have actually existed in the first place.

sections.title: The Three Core Memoization Tools
Why useCallback Is Almost Always Paired With React.memo, And Useless Without It
sections.content: This is the single most common, costly misunderstanding about these three tools: useCallback, on its own, provides essentially no benefit unless the function it returns is actually passed as a prop to a React.memo-wrapped component. Without React.memo on the receiving component, that component re-renders whenever its parent re-renders regardless of whether the function prop is a stable, memoized reference or a brand new one each time — meaning useCallback's entire purpose (providing a stable reference a memoized child can correctly compare against) goes completely unused. This directly extends lesson 1's React.memo and this lesson's useCallback into one combined, correctly-paired pattern: applying useCallback to a function passed to a non-memoized child component is a genuinely common, real-world mistake that adds useCallback's own overhead (the dependency comparison itself) while providing zero actual benefit, since the child re-renders unconditionally regardless.

sections.title: A Correctly Diagnosed And Correctly Applied Optimization, Start To Finish
sections.content: This walks through this lesson's actual recommended process — measure, diagnose, then apply the correctly-paired fix — rather than jumping straight to code:
sections.explanation: Without React.memo on ProjectCard, useCallback on handleDelete would be genuinely pointless, exactly per this lesson's internalWorking section — ProjectCard would still re-render on every keystroke regardless of whether onDelete's reference was stable, since an unmemoized component always re-renders when its parent does. With BOTH pieces correctly paired — React.memo on the child AND useCallback on the function passed to it — typing in the search box no longer causes any ProjectCard to re-render at all, since their props (including the now-stable handleDelete reference) genuinely haven't changed between renders, which is precisely what React.memo's shallow comparison can now correctly detect.

sections.title: Where Real Teams Actually Apply These Tools, And Where They Deliberately Don't
sections.content: Real, experienced React teams apply React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback selectively and deliberately, specifically in response to genuine, Profiler-measured performance problems — a long list (where re-rendering many items unnecessarily is genuinely expensive), an expensive calculation (sorting or filtering a large dataset) recalculated needlessly, or exactly this lesson's codeLesson's memoized-child-with-unstable-function-prop pattern. Real teams specifically avoid wrapping every single component in React.memo by default, or memoizing every value and function reflexively, precisely because Module 4's broader 'premature optimization' caution applies directly here: these tools have genuine costs, and applying them without measured justification is a recognizable, common sign of a developer optimizing based on assumption rather than evidence.

sections.title: Common Performance Optimization Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Applying useCallback to a function passed to a component that isn't wrapped in React.memo, gaining zero actual benefit while still paying useCallback's own overhead — directly this lesson's single most important, most common mistake.

2. Wrapping every component in React.memo by default, 'just in case', without any Profiler evidence of an actual re-render problem, adding real comparison overhead to components that never needed it.

3. Forgetting that React.memo's comparison is shallow — if a prop is an object or array recreated fresh on every render (even containing identical-looking data), React.memo's shallow comparison will still consider it 'different' and re-render anyway, unless that object/array itself is also memoized with useMemo.

4. Using useMemo for a genuinely cheap calculation that wasn't actually causing any measurable performance problem, adding the comparison and memory overhead of memoization without any real corresponding benefit.

5. Trusting intuition about which components are 'probably' re-rendering too often, rather than actually using the Profiler to confirm or rule this out with real evidence, exactly the mistake this lesson's entire framing exists to prevent.

sections.title: Evidence-Based Optimization As A Direct Extension Of This Curriculum's Debugging Discipline
sections.content: This lesson's central, repeated insistence on measuring before optimizing is a direct, specific application of the exact same evidence-based diagnostic discipline Module 10, lesson 7 taught for full stack debugging generally: gather concrete evidence (the Network tab, direct API testing, and now the Profiler) before forming a hypothesis about where a problem actually lives, rather than guessing based on intuition or a component's surface-level complexity. Premature, unmeasured optimization is, in an important sense, exactly the same mistake as unmeasured debugging — acting confidently on an assumption rather than genuine evidence — just applied to a performance concern rather than a correctness bug. Developing the discipline to always ask 'what does the Profiler actually show' before reaching for React.memo, useMemo, or useCallback is precisely the professional habit this lesson exists to build.

sections.title: Using The Profiler To Confirm An Optimization Actually Worked
sections.content: After applying a memoization fix (exactly this lesson's codeLesson's React.memo + useCallback pairing), re-recording the same interaction in the Profiler and confirming the previously-unnecessary re-renders genuinely stopped occurring is just as important as the initial diagnostic measurement — a memoization fix applied incorrectly (mismatched dependencies, a missing React.memo wrapper, a still-unstable object reference) can silently fail to actually solve the original problem while still adding its own overhead, and only directly re-measuring confirms whether the fix genuinely worked as intended, rather than merely appearing, by code inspection alone, like it should have.

checkpoints.question: What is this lesson's single most important rule regarding React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback?
options: Apply all three to every component and value by default, for maximum performance
Measure actual re-render behavior using the Profiler first, and apply these tools only in response to genuine, evidence-based performance problems, since each carries its own real overhead
These tools should never actually be used in any real application
Only useMemo is ever genuinely useful; React.memo and useCallback have no real value
checkpoints.explanation: This lesson's central rule is measuring first with the Profiler before applying any memoization tool, since each carries genuine overhead that can exceed the problem it's meant to solve if applied without real evidence.

checkpoints.question: A developer applies useCallback to a function passed as a prop to a child component, but that child component is not wrapped in React.memo. What is the actual effect of this useCallback usage?
options: It provides significant performance benefits regardless of the child's memoization status
It provides essentially no benefit, since the unmemoized child re-renders whenever its parent re-renders regardless of whether the function prop's reference is stable
It causes the application to crash
It automatically wraps the child in React.memo as a side effect
checkpoints.explanation: useCallback's value depends entirely on the receiving component being wrapped in React.memo; without that pairing, the child re-renders unconditionally regardless of the function prop's stability, making useCallback alone ineffective.

checkpoints.question: Why does React.memo's shallow comparison sometimes fail to prevent a re-render even when the underlying data 'looks' identical?
options: React.memo never actually works correctly

If a prop is an object or array recreated fresh on every render, the shallow comparison considers it a different reference even if its contents look the same, unless that value is also memoized with useMemo
Shallow comparison only works for string and number props, never objects
This only happens if the component has more than 10 props
checkpoints.explanation: React.memo's shallow comparison checks reference equality; a freshly recreated object or array, even with identical-looking contents, is a different reference and will be treated as changed unless explicitly memoized with useMemo.

codingChallenge.title: Diagnose And Correctly Fix An Unnecessary Re-Render Pattern
codingChallenge.description: Given a ProductList component where every ProductCard re-renders whenever an unrelated counter updates, apply the correctly-paired React.memo and useCallback fix, and write a comment explaining what the Profiler would show before and after the fix.
validationRules: ProductCard must be wrapped in React.memo
handleAddToCart must use useCallback with an empty dependency array
Both pieces must be correctly paired together - memo alone or useCallback alone would not be sufficient
Must include a comment explaining the specific before/after Profiler difference
hints: React.memo and useCallback must both be applied together to actually solve this specific problem - neither one alone is sufficient
handleAddToCart has no dependencies on anything that changes, so an empty dependency array is correct
The key insight to articulate: before the fix, EVERY ProductCard re-renders on every counter click; after, NONE do

lessons.title: Code Splitting And Lazy Loading
lessons.lessonGoal: Understand code splitting as a bundle-size optimization distinct from lesson 4's re-render optimizations, and apply React.lazy and Suspense to defer loading genuinely large or rarely-needed code.

sections.title: A Genuinely Different Kind Of Performance Problem
sections.content: Lesson 4's optimizations all addressed re-render performance: how often and how expensively components recompute their output once the application's JavaScript is already downloaded and running. Code splitting addresses a completely different, earlier-stage performance concern: how much JavaScript a user's browser must download and parse before the application can run AT ALL, directly extending Module 3's general performance-awareness theme to an application's overall bundle size. A large React application with many features, many pages, and many dependencies can accumulate a genuinely large total JavaScript bundle — code splitting breaks that one large bundle into smaller pieces, loaded only when actually needed, rather than forcing every single user to download the application's entire codebase just to view its first page.

sections.title: A Library That Hands You One Book At A Time, Not The Entire Collection Upfront
sections.content: Imagine a library that, before letting you read even the first page of any single book, required you to first carry home its ENTIRE collection — every book in the building — regardless of whether you intended to read more than one. This is exactly what a single, unsplit JavaScript bundle does: a user visiting only your application's home page still downloads the code for every other page and feature, whether or not they'll ever visit them. Code splitting is the library instead handing you only the specific book you actually asked for, with the option to request additional books later, exactly when and if you actually need them — dramatically reducing what you need to carry home (download) just to start reading (use the application) at all.

sections.title: React.lazy And Suspense
How import() Creates A Genuinely Separate Bundle, And Why That Matters
sections.content: A regular, static import (import AdminDashboard from './AdminDashboard') tells the build tool (the same bundler Module 10, lesson 5 used for production builds) to include that component's code directly in the main bundle, bundled together with everything else, evaluated and ready immediately. The dynamic import() function call inside React.lazy's argument is fundamentally different: it returns a Promise, and the build tool recognizes this specific pattern as a signal to split that component's code into its OWN separate file, only fetched over the network when that import() call actually executes at runtime — exactly the moment AdminDashboard genuinely needs to render for the first time. This is precisely why code splitting specifically targets genuinely large, conditionally-needed pieces of an application (an admin dashboard most users never visit, a complex chart library only needed on one specific page) rather than small, universally-needed pieces, where the overhead of a separate network request would outweigh any genuine bundle-size benefit.

sections.title: Code Splitting A Genuinely Large, Conditionally-Rendered Feature
sections.content: This applies lazy loading specifically to a route-level component, directly extending Module 13, lesson 2's file-based routing with a deliberate bundle-size optimization:
sections.explanation: A regular user, who will only ever render UserDashboard, never downloads AdminDashboard's code at all — it remains in its own separate bundle, simply never fetched, since that specific import() call never executes for that user. This is a direct, practical payoff for an application with genuinely distinct user roles (Module 9's authorization concept, applied here to bundle-size optimization specifically): the actual amount of code any given user downloads scales with what THEY genuinely use, rather than with the application's total combined feature set, regardless of relevance to that specific user.

sections.title: Where Real Applications Apply Code Splitting Deliberately
sections.content: Real, large production React applications commonly apply code splitting at route boundaries (each distinct page or major section becomes its own separate bundle, loaded only when a user actually navigates there — many React routing solutions and meta-frameworks like Module 13's Next.js handle a meaningful amount of this automatically, route by route) and for genuinely large, conditionally-used libraries (a complex charting library only needed on one analytics page, a rich text editor only needed on one content-creation page). Real teams typically measure bundle size directly (using bundle analysis tools that visualize exactly what's contributing to an application's total JavaScript size) before deciding where code splitting would genuinely help, directly extending lesson 4's 'measure before optimizing' discipline to this entirely different category of performance concern.

sections.title: Common Code Splitting Mistakes
sections.content:
1. Applying React.lazy to small, universally-needed components, where the overhead of an additional network request for that small piece outweighs any genuine bundle-size savings — code splitting pays off specifically for genuinely large or conditionally-needed code, not indiscriminately for everything.

2. Forgetting to wrap a lazily-loaded component in Suspense at all, resulting in a confusing error rather than the intended, graceful loading fallback while that component's separate bundle downloads.

3. Confusing lesson 4's re-render optimizations (React.memo, useMemo, useCallback) with this lesson's bundle-size optimization (React.lazy, code splitting) as if they solve the same problem — they address genuinely different performance concerns (recomputation cost versus initial download size) and neither substitutes for the other.

4. Code splitting so aggressively, at too fine a granularity, that an application ends up making an excessive number of small, separate network requests, potentially harming performance more than the unsplit bundle would have, rather than choosing genuinely large, meaningful split points.

5. Forgetting that a lazily-loaded component's Suspense fallback is shown EVERY time that specific code needs to be fetched for the first time in a user's session, and designing an unnecessarily jarring or unpolished loading state for what should be a brief, occasional moment.

sections.title: Two Genuinely Different Performance Concerns, Requiring Two Genuinely Different Tools
sections.content: This lesson's explicit distinction from lesson 4 — re-render cost versus initial bundle size — is a valuable, general engineering lesson in its own right: 'performance' is not one single, undifferentiated concern with one single fix; it's a category containing genuinely distinct sub-problems (how much code must be downloaded, how often does that code need to recompute its output, how efficiently does a database query execute, and others this curriculum has covered in Module 8) each requiring its own specific diagnostic approach and its own specific tool. Recognizing which SPECIFIC performance concern you're actually facing — and reaching for the tool genuinely suited to that specific concern, rather than treating 'performance optimization' as one undifferentiated activity — is precisely the kind of precise, deliberate engineering judgment this entire module has built toward.

sections.title: Diagnosing Bundle Size Problems Specifically
sections.content: If an application's initial page load feels slow specifically due to a large amount of JavaScript needing to download and parse before anything renders (a genuinely different symptom from lesson 4's re-render sluggishness, observable directly in DevTools' Network tab by checking the actual size and load time of JavaScript files), a bundle analyzer tool is the right diagnostic instrument — it visualizes exactly which dependencies and components contribute the most to an application's total bundle size, directly revealing the best, most impactful candidates for this lesson's code splitting technique, rather than guessing which components are 'probably' large based on their apparent complexity in source code alone.

checkpoints.question: What specific performance concern does code splitting address, distinct from lesson 4's React.memo/useMemo/useCallback?
options: Exactly the same concern as lesson 4's tools, just expressed differently
How much JavaScript a user's browser must download and parse before the application can run at all, distinct from how often already-loaded components recompute their output
Database query performance specifically
Code splitting only affects CSS, never JavaScript
checkpoints.explanation: Code splitting addresses initial bundle/download size, a genuinely different performance concern from lesson 4's re-render and recomputation optimizations.

checkpoints.question: An application uses React.lazy to code-split an AdminDashboard component, only rendered for users with an admin role. What happens for a regular, non-admin user?
options: They still download AdminDashboard's code, just don't see it rendered
They never download AdminDashboard's code at all, since the import() call for it never executes for a user whose role never triggers that component's rendering
The entire application fails to load for non-admin users
Code splitting has no effect on which code is actually downloaded
checkpoints.explanation: Since the dynamic import() only executes when the lazy component actually needs to render, a user who never renders that component never triggers the network request to download its separate bundle at all.

checkpoints.question: What kind of component is genuinely well-suited to code splitting, according to this lesson?
options: Every single component in an application, regardless of size or how often it's needed

Genuinely large or conditionally-needed code, such as an admin-only feature or a large library only needed on one specific page, where the bundle-size savings outweigh the overhead of an additional network request
Only components with no props at all
Code splitting should never actually be applied to any component
checkpoints.explanation: Code splitting pays off specifically for genuinely large or conditionally-needed code, where the bundle-size benefit outweighs the overhead of fetching it as a separate request, not for small or universally-needed pieces.

lessons.title: React In Production
lessons.lessonGoal: Synthesize composition, custom hooks, Context architecture, and performance optimization into a repeatable architectural review checklist for any growing React codebase, and develop the judgment for when added architectural complexity is genuinely justified.

sections.title: Closing The Loop: From Individual Techniques To Architectural Judgment
sections.content: Every prior lesson in this module taught one specific technique in isolation: composition patterns (lesson 1), custom hooks (lesson 2), Context architecture (lesson 3), re-render optimization (lesson 4), and bundle-size optimization (lesson 5). This closing lesson does what every module's final lesson in this curriculum has done since Module 1: synthesize these individually-correct techniques into one coherent, repeatable architectural review process, and — just as importantly — develop the judgment for recognizing when EACH technique's added complexity is genuinely justified by a real, current need, versus when it would be premature, unjustified architectural overhead for a project's actual current scale.

sections.title: A Building Inspector's Checklist, Now Specifically For React Architecture
sections.content: Module 7, lesson 10 introduced the building-inspector's checklist metaphor for backend code generally. This lesson is that exact same inspector, now walking through a React codebase specifically, checking: are components composed sensibly, or is one component trying to do everything through an ever-growing list of configuration props (lesson 1)? Is stateful logic appropriately extracted into custom hooks, or copy-pasted across multiple components (lesson 2)? Are contexts appropriately scoped, or one giant combined context causing unnecessary re-renders everywhere (lesson 3)? Are memoization and code splitting applied where genuine, measured evidence justifies them — or, just as importantly, are they ABSENT where they're not actually needed, avoiding unjustified complexity (lessons 4-5)? A genuinely production-ready React codebase passes every one of these checks deliberately, not by accident or by reflexively applying every available technique regardless of fit.

sections.title: The Five Recurring Architectural Checks From This Module
sections.content:
1. Composition Over Configuration (lesson 1) — does a component's prop list keep growing to handle new variations, signaling a genuine need for composition instead, or is composition already used appropriately where flexibility is genuinely needed?

2. Genuine Logic Extraction (lesson 2) — is the same useState/useEffect pattern duplicated across multiple components (a genuine signal for a custom hook), or has logic been extracted prematurely, before any real duplication existed?

3. Appropriately-Scoped Context (lesson 3) — are contexts split sensibly based on what actually changes together and who actually needs each piece, with measured evidence (the Profiler) behind any splitting decision, rather than either one giant combined context or excessive, unjustified fragmentation?

4. Evidence-Based Re-Render Optimization (lesson 4) — is every React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback usage backed by genuine Profiler evidence of a real problem, correctly paired (React.memo with useCallback specifically), rather than applied reflexively or incompletely?

5. Deliberate Bundle-Size Management (lesson 5) — is code splitting applied at genuinely large, conditionally-needed boundaries (an admin section, a heavy library), based on real bundle-analysis evidence, rather than either ignored entirely at real scale or over-applied at too fine a granularity?

sections.title: Applying The Checklist As A Genuine, Honest Architectural Review
sections.content: These five checks combine into a practical review process for any growing React codebase: for composition, scan recently-added props across the codebase's most frequently-modified components — a prop list that's grown by several new options over the project's recent history is a concrete signal worth investigating for a composition-based alternative. For logic extraction, search for near-identical useState/useEffect blocks across multiple files — genuine duplication, not superficial similarity, is the signal lesson 2 specifically called for. For Context scope, use the Profiler (lesson 3, lesson 4) to record a real interaction and check whether components unrelated to that interaction are nonetheless re-rendering. For memoization, audit every existing React.memo/useMemo/useCallback usage and ask, honestly, whether genuine Profiler evidence ever justified each one, or whether some were added speculatively. For bundle size, run an actual bundle analysis and identify the largest, least-frequently-needed pieces as the most justified code-splitting candidates. Every single check in this list demands actual, concrete evidence — a re-read of the code, a Profiler recording, a bundle analysis — never assumption alone.

sections.title: A Complete Architectural Review Of A Realistic Growing Feature
sections.content: Applying all 5 checks to a hypothetical 'team dashboard' feature that's grown organically over several months, before approving it as genuinely production-ready:
sections.explanation: Every single finding in this review traces directly back to one of this module's five lessons, and — critically, echoing this lesson's repeated emphasis on genuine evidence — every finding is backed by something concrete: an actual prop count, actual duplicated code, an actual Profiler recording, an actual bundle analysis. This is precisely the kind of honest, evidence-based review this lesson exists to model: not assuming a feature that 'works' is therefore architecturally sound, but actually walking through each of these five checks with real evidence before calling a feature genuinely production-ready.

sections.title: How This Architectural Review Mirrors Real Senior Engineering Practice
sections.content: Experienced React engineers conducting real code review or technical design discussions are, in practice, applying almost exactly this five-check process, often without consciously naming it this way — a reviewer noting 'this component's prop list is getting unwieldy, could this be composed differently' is applying check 1 directly; a reviewer asking 'did you actually profile this before adding memo here' is applying check 4 directly. Real engineering organizations increasingly value this kind of evidence-based architectural judgment specifically because React applications that grow without this kind of periodic, honest review tend to accumulate exactly the kinds of organically-grown problems this lesson's codeLesson example demonstrated — not because any single decision was unreasonable in isolation, but because no one stepped back to evaluate the accumulated whole against concrete evidence.

sections.title: What Happens Without This Kind Of Periodic Architectural Review
sections.content: React codebases that grow without this kind of periodic, evidence-based review accumulate exactly the problems this lesson's checklist is designed to catch: components with unwieldy, ever-growing prop lists that should have been composed differently; genuinely duplicated logic scattered across many files instead of consolidated into custom hooks; overly broad contexts causing widespread, hard-to-diagnose re-render problems; memoization applied speculatively without ever actually solving anything, or applied incompletely (missing its required pairing); and large, rarely-used code shipped to every single user regardless of need. These issues are all still fixable after the fact, but — echoing this curriculum's repeated argument about the cost of deferred quality work — cost considerably more to untangle once a codebase has grown substantially around these unreviewed, organically-accumulated decisions, compared to the relatively modest cost of this lesson's periodic, evidence-based review.

sections.title: Fundamentals Are Still The Real Curriculum, Now Applied To React's Own Internals
sections.content: This module's closing lesson continues this curriculum's most consistently recurring theme, now applied specifically to React's own architectural patterns rather than a new framework or language: composition over configuration, genuine-duplication-as-the-signal-for-extraction, evidence over assumption, and deliberate complexity matched to actual current need are not React-specific ideas at all — they are the exact same engineering judgment this curriculum has built since Module 4's DRY principle, Module 7's trust boundaries, and Module 10's production-thinking, now demonstrated concretely within React's own component and hook model specifically. A developer who's internalized this module's underlying judgment, rather than only memorized React.memo's syntax or useCallback's signature, can apply this same architectural discipline to any future framework's own specific patterns, recognizing the same underlying decisions wearing whatever new syntax that future framework happens to use.

sections.title: Auditing Your Own Module 14 Coding Challenges Against This Checklist
sections.content: The most direct way to internalize this lesson is to revisit every coding challenge built throughout this module — the compound Accordion, the useDebounce hook, the split Notifications/Settings contexts, the memoized ProductCard, the lazy-loaded AdvancedSettings — and walk each one through this lesson's five checks honestly: was each technique applied because genuine evidence justified it, or because the challenge simply asked for it? Would you, reviewing this same code without already knowing which lesson it came from, independently conclude each technique was genuinely warranted? Running this honest, retrospective audit on your own recent work is precisely what converts this lesson's five-check framework from an abstract list into a genuine, applied habit you'll carry into every future React codebase you build or review.

checkpoints.question: According to this lesson's framework, what is the common thread connecting all five architectural checks?
options: Every technique from this module should always be applied to every component, by default
Each technique's application should be backed by genuine, concrete evidence (actual duplication, actual Profiler data, actual bundle analysis), not assumption or reflexive habit
Only composition and custom hooks matter; the other three checks are unnecessary
Architectural review is unnecessary once a feature passes its initial tests
checkpoints.explanation: Every one of this lesson's five checks demands genuine, concrete evidence behind each architectural decision, rather than assumption, habit, or reflexive application of any specific technique.

checkpoints.question: A component was wrapped in React.memo six months ago, but a current Profiler recording shows it still re-renders on every parent render due to an unstable function prop. What does this lesson's review process reveal about this situation?
options: React.memo is broken and should be removed entirely
The memoization was applied incompletely - missing its required useCallback pairing (lesson 4) - and the review process catches this gap that casual code reading alone would likely miss
This is expected, normal behavior with no actual problem
Profiler evidence is unreliable and should not be trusted
checkpoints.explanation: This scenario demonstrates exactly the kind of gap this lesson's evidence-based review process is designed to catch - a memoization technique applied incompletely, only revealed through actual Profiler verification rather than assumed correctness from code inspection alone.

checkpoints.question: What is this lesson's central argument about why React codebases benefit from periodic, evidence-based architectural review?
options: Reviews are purely a formality with no genuine diagnostic value

Codebases that grow without this kind of review tend to accumulate organically-grown problems (unwieldy props, duplicated logic, overly broad contexts, incomplete optimizations) that are individually reasonable but costly to untangle once accumulated, making periodic review considerably cheaper than deferred correction
Architectural review is only necessary for codebases with more than 1000 components
Once a codebase passes its initial tests, no further architectural review is ever needed
checkpoints.explanation: The lesson argues that periodic, evidence-based review catches organically-accumulated architectural problems early and cheaply, compared to the higher cost of untangling them after a codebase has grown substantially around unreviewed decisions.

## Architectural Review

### 1. Composition check:
Reviewed my Accordion component - it correctly uses composition
(Accordion.Item, Accordion.Header, Accordion.Content) rather than a
growing list of configuration props. No issue found here.

### 2. Logic extraction check:
Found that my useFetch and useLocalStorage hooks both duplicate the
same try/catch error-message-extraction logic. This is genuine
duplication worth extracting into a shared helper function.

### 3. Context scope check:
My split NotificationsContext and SettingsContext are correctly
separated - confirmed via the Profiler that changing density never
re-renders any component consuming only NotificationsContext.

### 4. Memoization audit:
My ProductCard's React.memo and useCallback pairing was verified
correct via the Profiler - zero re-renders occur on unrelated counter
changes, confirming the optimization genuinely works as intended.

### 5. Bundle size check:
My AdvancedSettings lazy-loading was applied without ever actually
running a bundle analysis first - I should verify it's genuinely a
large enough component to justify the added complexity.

2. Run an actual bundle analysis on AdvancedSettings before considering

finalModuleProject.title: Architect And Audit A Production-Grade React Feature
finalModuleProject.goal: Synthesize everything from all 6 lessons — composition patterns, custom hooks, scoped Context, evidence-based memoization, and deliberate code splitting — by building one genuinely production-grade React feature, then conducting lesson 6's full architectural review against your own work with real, honest evidence.

Conclude with a full, honest 5-check architectural review of your own implementation, following lesson 6's exact process.
